 Breakfast food giant makes major change to iconic cereal's recipe
 Kellogg's is reformulating Rice Krispies overseas
 Facebook 
 Twitter 
 Threads 
 Print 
 Email 
 Add Fox Business on Google 
 By Brittany Miller FOXBusiness close video Kellogg's making cereal fun again with new cereal cafe 
 Snap, crackle and shop
 Kellogg's is changing the recipe for its iconic Rice Krispies cereal in the United Kingdom, replacing whole rice grains with rice flour as weather-related disruptions affect ingredient supplies.
 Kellanova, the company responsible for Kellogg's cereal brands outside North America, has also reformulated its Coco Pops — aka Cocoa Krispies in the U.S. — replacing whole rice grains with a combination of rice flour and corn flour, according to British grocery publication The Grocer.
 The changes will not affect Rice Krispies sold in the United States or Canada, WK Kellogg Co. confirmed to FOX Business.
 KELLOGG REMOVING ARTIFICIAL COLORS FROM FROOT LOOPS, APPLE JACKS A YEAR AHEAD OF SCHEDULE 
 A box of Kellogg's Rice Krispies cereal sits beside a bowl of the popular breakfast food. The company has reformulated the cereal's recipe in the U.K., but the U.S. version remains unchanged. (Tiffany Hagler-Geard/Bloomberg via Getty Images / Getty Images) 
 "Kellogg’s Rice Krispies cereals sold in the U.S. and Canada are not impacted by the recently reported recipe changes to Kellogg’s Rice Krispies and Kellogg’s Coco Pops cereals in the U.K.," a spokesperson for the company said in a statement.
 WK Kellogg Co. said its Rice Krispies, Cocoa Krispies and Frosted Krispies cereals sold in North America will continue to be made with real rice with no changes to their ingredients or recipes.
The two businesses separated in 2023, when the former Kellogg Company split into Kellanova and WK Kellogg Co. Mars acquired Kellanova in December 2025. Ferrero acquired WK Kellogg Co. in September 2025. 
 Kellanova said the reformulation is intended to maintain consistent product quality as changing weather conditions affect the availability and quality of certain grains.
 GENERAL MILLS DITCHES ARTIFICIAL COLORS IN LUCKY CHARMS, TRIX 
 A store's breakfast cereal aisle. (Jeffrey Greenberg/Universal Images Group via Getty Images / Getty Images) 
 The updated U.K. recipes also contain wheat gluten, making the cereals unsuitable for consumers with wheat allergies or celiac disease.
 The company said the cereals continue to meet British nutritional standards for fat, salt and sugar, while retaining their previous levels of fiber, vitamin D and iron.
 Rice Krispies sales have also declined in Britain, according to The Grocer, although the company has not linked the reformulation to falling sales.
 WK Kellogg is accelerating plans to eliminate artificial colors from its entire cereal portfolio by the end of 2026. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images / Getty Images) 
 Other major cereal makers have also been updating their recipes. General Mills announced in August that its U.S. cereals, including Lucky Charms and Trix, no longer contain certified synthetic colors .

 The company plans to eliminate those additives from its entire U.S. retail portfolio by the end of 2027.
 A representative for Kellanova, which oversees the U.K. cereal brands, did not immediately respond to FOX Business' requests for comment.
